n: In this lecture we will consider the topic of bone fracture and healing. First, the relevance of the topic. In 2019 more than 178 million new and 455 million existing fracture cases were recorded worldwide. In about 5–10 per cent of fractures, especially of long tubular bones, healing is delayed or a false joint, that is, nonunion, develops. Such a condition causes a large economic burden through repeat operations, prolonged rehabilitation and loss of working capacity. Most fractures heal in 6–8 weeks, but a significant proportion do not heal.

t: Aim of the lesson and outline
n: The aim of the lesson is to understand the reactive changes in bone tissue in response to a fracture and the stages of healing. The outline has three parts. First: the stages of inflammation, callus formation and remodelling, and the cells involved in them. Second: stem cells from the periosteum, bone marrow and muscle, and the main signalling pathways. Third: factors that impair healing, that is, age, diabetes, smoking and infection, and treatment approaches, including parathyroid hormone, that is, PTH.

What is a reactive, that is, functional, change? Bone tissue responds to the injury of a fracture with a coordinated regenerative process. This is the essence of the reactive changes in the topic of this lesson. The process depends on precise coordination in time and space of immune, vascular, nervous and skeletal signalling programmes. The classical stages: inflammation, callus formation and remodelling. At the end the temporary tissue is converted into lamellar bone. Attention: persistent inflammation, inadequate blood supply, infection or instability lead to delayed union or a false joint.

t: Fracture epidemiology and the clinical problem
n: Fracture epidemiology and the clinical problem. In the USA there are about 2 million fractures per year: almost half a million hospital admissions, 2.5 million physician visits and 180,000 nursing home admissions. Femoral fractures make up only 14% of all fractures, yet they account for the major part of cost and morbidity. A hip fracture costs about 35,000–54,000 dollars per case, and mortality within one year reaches 20–30%. Most fractures heal in 6–8 weeks, but a significant proportion do not heal. Delay and non-union increase cost and morbidity.

t: Quick question: the burden of fractures
n: Quick question: the burden of fractures. About what percentage of long bone fractures heal late or progress to non-union? Answer: about 5–10%. Systemic factors that worsen healing: diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obesity, smoking and sex hormone deficiency. Delayed union is usually diagnosed after about 3–6 months, non-union after about 6–9 months. Attention, risk of error: delayed union is not the same as non-union. In the former, biological activity in the callus often continues.

t: The classical three stages of healing
n: The classical three stages of healing. The first stage is inflammation: a haematoma forms and immune cells arrive. The second stage is callus formation: first soft, then hard callus. The third stage is remodelling: woven bone is replaced by lamellae. The stages overlap, that is, the next begins before the previous one has finished. Remodelling is the last and longest stage, in which temporary bone is replaced by mature lamellar bone.

According to Bikle, healing is divided into four phases. Phase one is haematoma and inflammation, about 5 days: the haematoma contains platelets, neutrophils and monocytes, and M1 macrophages start the inflammation. Phase two is soft callus, about 5 days: angiogenesis, chondrogenesis and osteogenesis begin. Phase three is hard callus, several weeks: chondrocytes mineralise. Phase four is remodelling: after 3–4 weeks, over months and years, the tissue is converted into lamellar bone.

Let us look at the duration of the phases. Phase one, haematoma, about 5 days. Phase two, soft callus, also about 5 days. Phase three, hard callus, several weeks. Phase four, remodelling, months and even years. The phases merge into one another: their boundaries are not sharp, and the processes partly run simultaneously. Age, diabetes mellitus, obesity and autoimmune diseases affect healing and increase the risk of non-union. Remodelling begins after 3–4 weeks and continues for months.

There are three sites where bone forms. The first site is along the periosteum; the process is intramembranous and no cartilage is needed. The second site is in the fracture gap; the process is endochondral, through cartilage. The third site is inside the bone marrow; the process is intramedullary and no cartilage is needed. The main source of cells for sites 1 and 2 is periosteal stem cells. Cells of site 3 come from bone marrow stem cells and from transdifferentiation of cortical osteocytes. Attention: an intramedullary pin eliminates site 3, which is why it is little studied.

Attention: intramembranous bone formation is not the same as endochondral. Intramembranous bone formation proceeds along the periosteal surface and does not require an intermediate cartilage stage. Endochondral bone develops in the bridging zone between the fracture ends: first cartilage forms, then it is replaced by bone. Intramedullary bone forms inside the marrow, at the fracture ends. It, too, proceeds without an intermediate cartilage stage. Risk of error: do not think that bone formation without cartilage is only intramembranous; the intramedullary route is also cartilage-free.

Case analysis: intramedullary nail. Situation: a long bone fracture is fixed with an intramedullary nail. The nail occupies the marrow cavity and in effect eliminates it. If the marrow cavity is lost, there is no room for site 3, that is, for new bone formation inside the marrow. For this reason this site has often been overlooked. In mice, intramedullary bone begins on days 5–10, is temporary, and has almost disappeared by about day 28. Question: in a fracture with a nail, at which sites is bone formation preserved and at which is it hindered? Justify the answer.

Phase one: haematoma and platelets. In a fracture, blood vessels rupture and a haematoma forms. As a temporary matrix, it starts the repair. Platelets aggregate quickly, stopping the bleeding, and release growth factors and cytokines. These substances attract inflammatory cells and mesenchymal stromal cells, that is, MSC, to the fracture site. The haematoma is formed by erythrocytes and platelets, and neutrophils and monocytes enter it from the marrow. This phase lasts about 5 days.

The sequence of cells in phase one is as follows. After the haematoma forms, neutrophils enter the site of injury within a few hours. Monocytes enter the haematoma, become macrophages and change their activation state. Early M1 macrophages in the hypoxic haematoma release inflammatory cytokines. Then M2 macrophages support repair. So the chain is: haematoma and platelets, neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, then the switch from M1 to M2.

Remember: M1 is the cleaner and guard, M2 is the builder and soother. This brief mnemonic is based on the functions given in the source. Early M1 macrophages clear the tissue and protect against microbes. Later M2 macrophages quench inflammation and support angiogenesis. M2 macrophages release interleukin-10, that is, IL-10, reducing inflammation, and through VEGF, that is, vascular endothelial growth factor, support vessel formation. Attention: M1 and M2 are not strictly two separate groups. This is a simplified scheme, used as a convenient shorthand for describing the functional transition.

Other immune cells are also important. Regulatory T cells, that is, Treg, restrain excessive inflammation and maintain an immune state that supports repair. Mast cells may influence vascular permeability, leukocyte recruitment and local immune activity. MSC also suppress inflammation: through direct contact and TGFβ they induce Treg. Dendritic cells and B cells may modulate the adaptive immune response and osteoclast-related remodelling.

Case analysis: prolonged inflammation. The situation is a teaching example: there is infection at the fracture site, inflammation does not subside, and healing cannot progress to the repair stage. If tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-1β and IL-6 persist for long, inflammatory macrophages remain active and osteogenesis and angiogenesis are suppressed. Attention: the appearance of callus on radiography does not in itself prove either the presence of infection or the ability to heal. Question: why is it dangerous to suppress cytokines completely, and to what outcome, that is, non-union, can prolonged inflammation lead?

Phase two: soft callus and angiogenesis. Periosteal progenitors become osteoblasts or chondrocytes and form callus. In an oxygenated, stable site the osteoblast direction is chosen; under hypoxia or strain, the chondrocyte direction. The chain: haematoma and inflammation, proliferation of periosteal progenitors, angiogenesis, that is, capillary ingrowth, chondrogenesis, that is, soft callus, then mineralisation and hard callus. New capillaries deliver oxygen and nutrients, ensuring the transition from soft to hard callus.

t: Factors determining cell fate in the callus
n: Factors determining cell fate in the callus. With oxygen and stability, cells become osteoblasts; in hypoxia, chondrocytes. With oxygen and stability, osteogenesis occurs and intramembranous bone forms on the cortical surface. In hypoxia or strain, chondrogenesis proceeds and cartilaginous soft callus appears. Runx2 governs the osteogenic programme, that is, osteoblast development, and Sox9 the chondrogenic programme, that is, the chondrocyte. Some hypertrophic chondrocytes may join the osteoblast pool.

Quick question: hypoxia and callus. Under what conditions do mesenchymal stromal cells at the fracture site form cartilage, and under what conditions bone directly? In oxygen-rich and mechanically stable sites, MSC take the osteogenic route. Intramembranous bone forms on the cortical surface. In a hypoxic or mechanically strained site, MSC choose the chondrogenic programme. As a result, cartilaginous, that is, soft, callus forms and strengthens the fracture. Attention: endochondral is not the same as intramembranous. Intramembranous and intramedullary bone form without a cartilage stage, whereas cartilage is found in the bridging zone.

t: Phase 3: from soft callus to hard callus
n: Phase three: the transition from soft callus to hard callus. The third phase lasts several weeks. Cartilage is removed and calcified, and hard callus forms more fully. Chondrocytes mineralise. They are removed by osteoclasts, or they become osteoblasts. The process goes together with vascularisation. In hypertrophic chondrocytes sox9 and type X collagen fall, runx2 and β-catenin rise; then alkaline phosphatase, osterix, osteopontin and osteocalcin appear. MMP13 degrades the matrix, while noggin must fall. Woven bone forms first; in phase 4 it is replaced by lamellar bone.

Blood vessels: VEGF and HIF, that is, osteoangiogenesis. After a fracture, hypoxia appears. In hypoxia, HIF-1α, that is, hypoxia-inducible factor, is stabilised and switches on VEGF. VEGF, that is, vascular endothelial growth factor, through VEGFR2 brings about endothelial proliferation and vessel formation. As a result vessels enter the callus. Type H vessels are linked with osteoprogenitors; this has been established mainly in experimental models.

Phase four: remodelling. Remodelling is the last and longest stage of healing. Temporary woven bone is gradually replaced by mature lamellar bone. This process begins 3–4 weeks after the fracture and extends over months. The aim is to return the bone to its pre-fracture state, including restoration of haematopoietic and trabecular structures. In human bone, over time the Haversian system, that is, the central blood canal and the network of canaliculi, is re-formed.

Remodelling cells. The cycles of resorption and formation are linked; bone adapts to mechanical load. The osteoclast resorbs mineral and matrix. Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells of haematopoietic origin. The osteoblast secretes osteoid and mineralises it. The osteocyte is a mechanosensor: through the canaliculi it senses strain and microdamage and directs the work of other cells. The lining cell covers the inactive surface.

The RANKL and OPG axis. RANKL is produced by osteoblasts, osteocytes, stromal cells and T cells. It binds to RANK on osteoclast precursors and initiates osteoclastogenesis. OPG is a decoy receptor: it captures RANKL and limits osteoclast formation. The ratio of RANKL to OPG determines the net direction of turnover. It is influenced by Wnt and β-catenin, oestrogen status and inflammatory cytokines. Attention: RANKL is not OPG. RANKL enhances resorption, whereas OPG limits it; what matters is the ratio of the two.

Osteoclast and osteoblast coupling: ephrin, S1P, Sema3A. RANKL binds to RANK on the osteoclast precursor and, through NF-κB, NFATc1 and MAPK, starts resorption. Forward signalling through EphB4 on the osteoblast stimulates matrix assembly, while reverse signalling through ephrinB2 on the osteoclast suppresses NFATc1-dependent osteoclastogenesis. S1P, from osteoclasts and endothelium, attracts the osteoblast to the resorption site and supports its survival. Sema3A, mainly from osteoblasts and osteocytes, inhibits osteoclast differentiation and increases osteoblast activity.

t: Matrix degradation: MMP, TIMP and ADAMTS
n: Matrix degradation: MMP, TIMP and ADAMTS. For the callus to become load-bearing bone, balanced matrix degradation is needed; it is governed by the proteases MMP and ADAMTS. MMP-9 ensures vessel entry and cartilage removal, and MMP-13 the cartilage-to-bone transition. MMP-2 assists further matrix refinement. TIMPs limit MMP activity; ADAMTS4/5 cleave aggrecan. If proteolysis is insufficient, vessel entry and cartilage clearance are delayed; if it is excessive or untimely, the new tissue is unstable.

t: Case analysis: remodelling and a drug
n: Case analysis: remodelling and a drug. Situation: the fracture callus is at the remodelling stage. The doctor wants to choose a standard drug that suppresses the osteoclast. In remodelling, the osteoclast breaks down old tissue and the osteoblast forms new lamellar bone. These two processes are linked. In animal studies, PTH, that is, parathyroid hormone, outperformed antiresorptives such as alendronate. Clinical results are not uniform. Question: why might suppression of the osteoclast interfere with the conversion of callus into mature bone?

Sources of skeletal stem and progenitor cells. Periosteal stem cells are the main source in long bone repair; they are located in the inner cambium layer. In adults, LepR+ cells of the bone marrow, that is, perivascular stromal cells, are one of the main sources of osteoblasts. Muscle also contributes, that is, an auxiliary source, through FAP cells, whereas Pax7 satellite cells appear insignificant.

Main signalling pathways. Signals are phase-specific: one pathway acts differently at early and late stages. The result is determined not by quantity but by timing, receptor type and cell. TNF and interleukins act early, then in the repair phase, ensuring the transition from inflammation to repair. SDF-1 and CXCR4 act early, in hypoxia, attracting progenitors to the fracture site. TGF-β, BMP and Wnt in the middle and late phases govern cell direction and bone maturation. Hedgehog and Notch regulate the pace of the cartilage-to-bone transition. If Wnt is excessively activated prematurely, it may suppress the intermediate cartilage stage.

Mechanical factors and mechanotransduction. Controlled strain supports callus formation and maturation. Instability, load protection, that is, stress shielding, or prolonged absence of load disturb callus structure and healing. Osteocytes are mechanosensors: through the lacuno-canalicular network they sense strain and fluid shift and direct osteoblast and osteoclast activity. Where there is load, YAP and TAZ, that is, mechanosensitive transcription factors, move to the nucleus and switch on osteogenic genes; without load they remain in the cytoplasm.

Impaired healing and clinical phenotypes. In delayed union, after about 3–6 months there is not enough growth, although biological activity is often present. Non-union is diagnosed at about 6–9 months; the criterion of the US Food and Drug Administration, that is, FDA: at least 9 months, with 3 months without growth. If prolonged, a false joint, that is, pseudarthrosis, forms: a mobile fibrous layer. Types of non-union: hypertrophic, in which there is much callus but no bridge; atrophic, in which there is very little callus; oligotrophic, with intermediate features; and low-quality union, in which there is continuity but little strength.

t: Systemic factors impairing healing: ageing and hormones
n: Systemic factors impairing healing: ageing and hormones. With ageing, the osteogenic capacity of MSC decreases, Wnt and β-catenin, IGF-1 and BMP/TGF-β signalling change, and mechanotransduction and the angiogenic response weaken. Result: callus mineralisation is slow and the vascular and anabolic response weak; risk of delayed union and low-quality regenerate. In sex hormone deficiency, the balance of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, RANKL and OPG, oxidative stress and NF-κB change; through sclerostin, Wnt is weakened. In oestrogen deficiency models, callus delay, mineral accumulation and mechanical recovery may be incomplete.

Factors impairing healing. Age: the cellular and vascular response weakens, with risk of delayed union. Diabetes: impaired microcirculation, little vascular factor, callus small and poorly mineralised. Infection: persistent inflammation and vascular disturbance, resulting in non-union. Instability: excessive movement and shear strain, resulting in hypertrophic non-union and a false joint. The factors disrupt the coherence of inflammation, vasculature, cell recruitment and remodelling. Attention: the effect of NSAIDs, that is, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, is mixed; it depends on dose and duration. Smoking and open fracture raise the risk.

t: Attention: radiographic union ≠ full mechanical recovery
n: Attention: radiographic union is not full mechanical recovery. Union of low quality in mechanical terms is possible: continuity is restored, but the new part is weak, that is, has low mineral density, altered microarchitecture or low strength. Such a defect may be barely noticeable on a plain radiograph. In the long term it may impair the mechanical performance of the bone. Osteocytes sense strain and microdamage, so the mechanical environment and the quality of healing are linked. Attention: rapid radiographic union does not mean good bone quality. In brain injury, callus may form quickly, but bone quality may not be optimal.

t: Case analysis: a patient with diabetes who smokes
n: Case analysis: a patient with diabetes who smokes. Situation: in a smoker with diabetes the callus is small, poorly mineralised, with few vessels, and remodelling is delayed. In diabetes the AGE receptor is activated, oxidative stress rises, VEGF falls and microvessels are damaged. Smoking reduces callus perfusion, disrupts the coupling of osteoangiogenesis, shrinks the callus and lowers its mechanical strength. Question: which phases, 2 to 4, and which mechanism, that is, vessel entry, mineralisation or remodelling, are impaired? What is the risk of non-union?

Treatment: PTH and abaloparatide. Teriparatide, that is, PTH 1–34, and abaloparatide may accelerate healing; they share the same receptor. Clinical results are not uniform: in some trials healing was accelerated, but the number of non-unions did not fall. The anabolic effect acts mainly through the cAMP and PKA pathway; the Ca²⁺ and PKC pathway is linked with the catabolic effect. Wnt increases periosteal cambium cells. IGF1 is necessary for the anabolic effect of PTH. EfnB2 and EphB4 serve cell-to-cell communication and angiogenesis.

Experience with PTH and abaloparatide. Teriparatide, PTH 1–34, is effective in accelerating fracture healing in animal studies and some clinical studies, but the FDA has not approved it for this purpose in humans. In the 41 animal studies in the Gorter review, PTH outperformed antiresorptives such as alendronate: callus, strength and healing index were better. Clinical results are not uniform: in some studies healing was accelerated, but the number of non-unions did not fall. Abaloparatide is a synthetic 36-amino-acid analogue of PTHrP, with 76 % homology; it is more selective for the RG form of the PTH receptor, so the anabolic effect is stronger and the catabolic weaker.

Conclusion and consolidation. Healing proceeds in 4 stages: haematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodelling. The first two take about 5 days, the last lasts months and years. In a long bone, new bone forms at 3 sites: along the periosteum, between the fracture ends and inside the marrow. Stem cells come from the periosteum, marrow and muscle, with the periosteum the main source. In remodelling, the osteoclast resorbs woven bone and the osteoblast restores lamellar bone. Persistent inflammation, vascular insufficiency, infection, instability, diabetes and smoking delay healing. Treatment: growth factors, cell and gene therapy.
